name: Article I Dissenters
overview: The Article I Dissenters argue for the constitutional order the founders built: Congress declares war, lays tariffs, writes sanctions and oversees the money, and the president executes the laws Congress passes. Ambition should counter ambition, so a Republican Congress owes a Republican president the same checks it would apply to a Democrat. The program runs across issues: war-powers votes on Iran and Venezuela, ending the Canada tariff emergency, Fed independence, enforcing the Graham sanctions law Trump waived, and forcing out the Epstein files. Its libertarian wing adds restraint abroad and smaller government at home.

What sustains it is insulation and a small libertarian money network, not a donor class. Tillis is retiring, Murkowski and Paul do not face voters until 2028, and Collins's Maine trades heavily with Canada. Jeff Yass has supplied about 95% (~$35M over five years) of Protect Freedom PAC, built by Rand Paul's advisers; it funded Kentucky First ($1.4M for Massie), and Young Americans for Liberty funded another $1.1M. Kentucky 4th PAC's $6.6M came from a new dark-money group (Tamarack Aspen; a straw-donor complaint is pending). The outside wing (Massie, Greene) now lives on audience: Greene left the party (Jun 22) and Massie appears with Carlson ('The movement has begun', Aug 1).

Acts depart from words most where seats are at stake. The Senate core is three votes (Murkowski, Collins, Paul on May 13); Young and Hawley flipped on Venezuela after assurances (Jan 14); the 50-48 Iran win (Jun 23) reversed to 49-50 (Sep 24). Collins votes against tariffs and takes Maine carve-outs, and votes for war-powers limits while taking $100K+ in one quarter from defense-contractor PACs as Appropriations chair. The price of dissent is documented: about $15.5M went against Massie and he lost.

Precedent: Robert Taft's Senate Republicans, who fought Truman's undeclared Korean war on constitutional grounds (1950-51). It breaks because Taft led his party's Senate wing and nearly won the 1952 nomination, while today's dissenters are retiring, losing primaries or leaving the party, and the outside wing's leverage is a third-party threat rather than a nomination path (my reading).

Massie lost his primary on May 19, 54.9-45.1, to Ed Gallrein, whom Trump endorsed. For Massie, Kentucky 4th PAC spent $6.6M (from a dark-money group), Kentucky First $1.4M (Yass-funded Protect Freedom PAC) and Make Liberty Win $1.1M (FEC data via WKMS, Jul 17). Motives: conviction with a cost; the cost is now his outside platform.
Boebert, Mace, Norman Motives: Base pressure: their voters believe in a cover-up (reported).

Say versus do. The 218 commitments are claimed and unverified; the first petition is the act.

Why the faction does it. The worldview: an undeclared war past the 60-day clock violates Article I. The interest: the members who vote yes are insulated (Paul and Murkowski until 2028) or have already lost (Massie).
Who and why.
Murkowski: 'a timeline that has taken us beyond the 60 days' (May 13). Posture and interest match.
Paul: consistent yes; his network is funded by Yass through Protect Freedom PAC, which rewards the brand.
Collins: yes votes on the statute, while taking defense-contractor PAC money as Appropriations chair; the vote does not touch the spending she controls (my reading).
Massie and Greene: the outside wing. The war is their case against Trump and the content of their new platform with Carlson.
Say versus do. The core is three senators; Hawley and Curtis voiced 60-day concerns and voted no (May 13).

Stance audit. Members repeatedly sought war-powers votes while the coalition and vote counts shifted. Compare the May 13, June 23 and September 24 votes by member. The aggregate counts do not establish individual flips. Congressional authority and political independence are stakes. Yass-backed support applies to the libertarian wing. Credit repeated procedural action. Test individual consistency and electoral costs against roll calls.

paras: Position.
Feb 11: ended the Canada emergency 219-211. Oct 23: Collins won Maine carve-outs.
Why the faction does it. Two groups: free-trade conviction and electoral relief.
Who and why.

Collins voted repeatedly to halt the Canada tariffs and lobbied for a wood-products exemption for a border paper mill. She skipped Vance’s Maine events. Canada took about 40% of Maine’s $3.2B exports and supplies about 70% of its imports, the most trade-dependent state analyzed, and Canada dropped seafood from its Sep 8 counter-tariff list (NPR, Aug 31). Motives: (1) Re-election against Troy Jackson in a state that loses from the tariffs. (2) Distance: skipping Vance keeps her off the same stage as the unpopular policy (my reading). (3) Contractor PACs (GEO, CoreCivic) also gave to her; no link to a vote is shown.
Massie, Bacon, Kiley, Hurd, Newhouse, Paul, McConnell, Murkowski Motives: Free-trade conviction (reported). Several are retiring or insulated; the cost is low.
Say versus do. Collins votes against the principle and takes the exemption for her state.

paras: Position.

Trump posted that Hawley, Paul, Collins, Murkowski and Young should “never be elected to public office again.”
Jan 14: the vote was 50-50 and Vance broke the tie to block it.
Why the faction does it. Restraint and oversight of military action.
Who and why.

Hawley voted to advance the resolution on Jan 8, then flipped. He cited Rubio’s assurance of no ground troops or occupation and said sticking would mean he “wasn’t really serious.” Motives: (1) Pressure: Trump’s public attack came between the two votes. (2) Ambition: 2028 speculation around him means he cannot afford a fight with Trump (my reading). (3) He got a cover story he could repeat.
Young flipped after assurances (reported). Motives: Pressure and cover: the White House bought the vote with assurances.
Paul, Murkowski Motives: Conviction: consistent votes (reported). Neither moved.
Collins Motives: Re-election: a tight race in Maine against Democrat Troy Jackson (reported).
Say versus do. The flip shows that stated positions here can be bought; Paul and Murkowski did not move.
